intro: Stanton upon Hine Heath is a small village in north Shropshire, among farmland and woods between Shrewsbury and Market Drayton. In a wood near Hazels Road a reader found an oak with a limb that curls out from the trunk and grows back into it, closing a ring of wood, and sent us four photographs of it. Nobody they asked, they write, had seen that on any other tree.

trees.story:
"This is an oak tree that has a branch entering the tree to form a circle of wood," wrote the reader who sent it to us from a wood near Stanton upon Hine Heath in north Shropshire. "Totally natural but everyone asked has not seen this phenomenon on any other tree. To me it's a very special oak."

Their four photographs show exactly what they mean. Partway up, one of the oak's limbs leaves the trunk, curls out and round, and grows back into the tree a little higher, closing a ring of wood you can see the sky through. Trees do sometimes graft onto themselves where two of their own branches press together and fuse, which foresters call inosculation, but a whole loop like this is rare enough to stop people on the path.

Otherwise it is a woodland oak, moss on its lower trunk, rising among birches and younger trees, its crown holding the last brown leaves in the November pictures. We do not know its age or girth, or which oak it is; tell us here if you do.

Our pin marks the area. Look up as you walk, and the ring finds you.
